subtitle: The Establishment
title: DER STELLENPLAN
preamble:
The ministry's establishment return for 1970 went across to the Finance
Ministry sealed, as it does every year. It proposed three posts in the typing
pool for abolition at the turn of the year.

Before the envelope was opened, Fräulein Bühl applied for a post at the
Landschaftsverband. She is one of the three. She will say only that she had
been thinking about it for a while, which is not true, and everybody can hear
that it is not true.

What follows is everything that was found or said.
question: How did Fräulein Bühl come to know what was in the return? Fill in the report.

lines: The ribbon on Frau Pohlmann's machine has scarcely been used. She put it in the day after the return went across to the Finance Ministry.
Frau Pohlmann typed the return herself with the door shut, which she does with anything that has names in it, and she did not give it to the pool.
Herr Grau did not deal with the pool and would not have known which of the typists Fräulein Bühl was. Anything for the pool went through the outer office on paper.

The door between his room and the outer office stands open, as it always has, and Frau Pohlmann's desk is what he sees when he looks up. The girl from the pool has never once come in at her door, and Frau Pohlmann does not go out to the landing while the girl is there; he would see her go.

The basket from the outer office of 407 goes into the same sack as the rest of the fourth floor, and the sack stands on the landing until the collection, because the back stair is too narrow to take it down with the trolley.

The pension file on Herr Simon's counter, where the girls leave it: at the page on the marriage refund, a printed slip from the pension office pasted over it: repealed, with effect from the start of last year.
The return went across sealed and the seal was broken at the Finance Ministry. Herr Simon never had it open.
Pinned into the loan book beside the entry for the return: the Finance Ministry's receipt for one envelope under the seal of the Personalreferat, signed for over there, the seal taken in unbroken.

The loan book has a column for enclosures and Herr Simon fills it in for everything, a sealed return too: in this house it is entered here before he carries it down to the post room himself. The entry for the return says three.
Fräulein Bühl signed the book that week for a file about a pension that was nothing to do with her, and the book was open on the counter where it always is.

The pool's work book: nothing from 407 entered in the week the return was typed. Everything from 407 in it, in any week, is entered as from the outer office, and not one line asks for a typist by name.

The Dienstaltersliste is pinned by the door and brought up to date every January. It is not an Entlassungsliste and everybody in the room knows that the distinction has never saved the last names on it.
The new ribbons come on two spools in a tin and there is a requisition for them, and the requisition asks how many were used last quarter, and nobody has ever been able to answer it.
The pencil sharpener on the window sill has been broken since September and there is no form for a pencil sharpener.

The new machines are lighter to strike and Frau Litt does not think that is an improvement, because a light touch lets you type faster than you can think. There are two of them so far, and they take the new ribbons that run through once; the rest of the pool is still on cloth.
Frau Litt had Fräulein Bühl up at that window with a spent ribbon inside a week of her starting, the same as she does with all of them, and Fräulein Bühl was politer about it than most of them are.

The girls who are getting married all go down to the Registratur for the pension file and look up the marriage refund, the money you used to get back from your pension when you married, and it was done away with at the start of last year and nobody ever tells them.
She heard about the return when everybody else did and was put out about it, and being put out about not knowing a thing first is the one thing she cannot act.
Her elder boy has finished and the younger one has not, and she tells you which of them she worries about and it is not the one you expect.
Coal has gone up again and she says the figure, and it is right.

She holds a spent ribbon up against the window for anybody in the pool who will stand still, and reads off it what was typed on it, and thinks it a scandalous waste to throw out a ribbon that has only been through the machine once.

She has not been up to the fourth floor in years and does not mean to start, so it is the newest girl in the pool who brings her down the spoiled sheets out of the fourth-floor sack, and only the sheets, because a sheet with a clean back is still half a sheet.
Frau Adam heard about the return the same morning as the rest of the pool, and was put out about it all week, which with Frau Adam you can see from across the room.
When it finally came out which three posts had gone, two of them belonged to women who were nowhere near the bottom of the list, and the room has not finished being astonished about it.
Herr Grau has never once sent down for a girl by name in all the years she has had this room. It is always a typist, and it is always through the outer office.
The cloth ribbons went round and round and you used them until they were grey, and she can still tell you what a box of them cost in 1953, to the Pfennig, without being asked.

She changes her own ribbon and always has, and the old one goes in her basket with everything else. The outer office was given the new ribbons before the pool was, and she has had no cloth ribbon in her machine since the winter.
She has taken her half hour at her own desk for eleven years. The pool eats in the canteen. In eleven years she has not once been down there.
The pool's post goes out on the table on the landing. The girl who comes up for it has never been inside her door, and Frau Pohlmann is not at the table when she comes.

Frau Litt used to come up to this floor to argue about ribbons in person, and she has not done it since the pool was given a requisition of its own. She has not been on the fourth floor in years; she would not come up without looking in at this door.
Herr Grau did not deal with the pool and would not have known which of the typists Fräulein Bühl was. Anything for the pool went through this desk, on paper.

She is the last out of this floor most evenings and so she sees the cleaners come in: never before the pool has gone home, the charwoman with them, and gone again before anybody arrives in the morning.
Eleven years in that outer office and three Referatsleiter, and the first of them wrote everything in longhand and she typed from it, and she thought at the time that this was the last of something.

He has eaten in the canteen every working day for twenty years, and in all that time Frau Pohlmann has not once come down to it. The morning the return was first talked of at the pool's table, Frau Adam was the one asking everybody what it was.

When he takes files up to 407 the pool's girl is as often as not at the table on the landing for the post, and he has never seen her go in at Frau Pohlmann's door, or Frau Pohlmann come out to the table.
The stairs and the paternoster both pass the landing outside his counter. He sees the newest girl go up for the post most days, and he has not seen Frau Litt go up in years.
Asked what the enclosure column counts, he says whatever is in the envelope, and that it is there so a thing that goes out with three comes back with three, and that it has never meant anything else.
Files go out on the book and come back on the book, and roughly one a month does not, and each one of those he remembers.

He locks the Registratur last thing. By then the pool is long gone, every one of them down the stairs past his counter, and the cleaners come up past it while he turns the key, the charwoman with them. In the morning he is at his counter before any of the pool comes in, and the cleaners have been and gone.
Whoever is newest in the pool fetches the post from the fourth floor, and has done since before anybody can remember, and she is newest.
She is to be married next spring and means to go on working, which her mother thinks is a phase.
She will not use the paternoster and takes the stairs, and says so without being asked, the way people do about the things that frighten them.

She asked Herr Simon once, while he was locking up, why the thrown-out ribbons have the letters cut out of them in a row, and he showed her: the bar swings up, the ribbon is between it and the paper, and what the blow lifts off the ribbon is what comes out on the sheet.
Frau Pohlmann tears her spoiled sheets up small before they go in the basket, every one of them, which nobody else in this building does, and it is the devil to get the pieces out of the corners.
Out of Frau Pohlmann's basket, every few weeks, the ribbon she has taken off her machine: the new shiny sort, not the cloth ones the pool throws out. It goes in the sack with the rest.
She carries out what is in the baskets and does not read any of it, and would not have made much of it if she had, and says so without any embarrassment at all.
The trolley has a wheel that turns sideways and there is a form for it, and she has filled the form in twice.

She has cooked for this building for nine years and serves at the hatch herself, and knows everybody who eats here by what they take. The pool comes down together and sits at the long table by the radiator. Frau Pohlmann from 407 she knows by sight, from the stairs, and has never once served.
After five she counts the day's meal tickets into bundles of fifty, and one bundle is always one short, and she has stopped minding which.

The pool goes down to the canteen together, past his window, and the outer office does not go at all. Frau Pohlmann has her tray carried up to her, and has had it so as long as he has been on the door.

He lets the cleaning women in at the side door himself, and not one of them has come in while anybody from the pool was still in the building: the pool goes out past his window first, and he sees to it. In the morning they are out again before the first of the pool is at the door.

dossiers.de: Ministerialrat, Mitte fünfzig, im Haus seit dem Umzug. Er hört einem bis zum Ende zu und entscheidet dann, was er ohnehin entschieden hatte, und hält beides für dasselbe. Ein Mann, der Namen nie vergisst und Gesichter schon. Er redet über die Arbeit wie über das Wetter: sachlich, unaufhörlich und ohne dass jemand klüger wird. Zu Hause wird er anders sein, sagt das Haus, und das Haus weiß es nicht.
dossiers.en: Ministerialrat, in his middle fifties, in the building since the move. He hears you out and then decides what he had decided already, and considers those the same thing. A man who never forgets a name and does forget faces. He talks about work the way other people talk about weather: steadily, at length, and without anybody coming away wiser. He must be different at home, the building says, and the building does not know.

dossiers.de: Fünfundvierzig, seit elf Jahren die Schreibkraft des Personalreferats, drei Referenten lang; ihr Zimmer nennt das Haus das Vorzimmer. Frau, nicht Fräulein, und niemand im Haus könnte sagen, wann das angefangen hat. Sie ist die Einzige, die weiß, was ihr Chef wirklich meint, wenn er nichts sagt, und sie sagt es nicht weiter. Höflich zu allen, vertraut mit keiner; die Damen aus dem Saal grüßt sie freundlich und beim Nachnamen. Sie hat einen Mantel für den Winter und einen für den Herbst und trägt beide, bis sie nicht mehr gehen.
dossiers.en: Forty-five, eleven years the Personalreferat's own typist, three Referenten, in a room the house has always called by a grander name than the rules give it. Frau, not Fräulein, and nobody in the building could tell you when that began. She is the only person who knows what her chief means when he says nothing, and she does not pass it on. Civil to everybody and close to nobody; she greets the women from the pool kindly and by their surnames. She has one coat for winter and one for autumn and wears each until it will not do.

dossiers.de: Vierundfünfzig, Registraturvorsteher, seit zwanzig Jahren in der Registratur, und er sagt jeden Satz so, als hätte er ihn schon zwanzig Jahre gesagt, was stimmt. Ordnung ist bei ihm keine Tugend, sondern eine Gewohnheit, die er sich nicht mehr abgewöhnen könnte. Er verwechselt nie eine Nummer und selten einen Namen. Wenn etwas nicht zurückkommt, ärgert er sich still und lange. Sein Bruder hatte eine Gastwirtschaft, und davon erzählt er einmal im Jahr.
dossiers.en: Fifty-four, twenty years in the Registratur, and he says every sentence like a man who has been saying it for twenty years, which he has. Order is not a virtue with him but a habit he could no longer break. He never mixes up a number and rarely a name. When something does not come back he is quietly and lastingly annoyed. His brother kept an inn, and he tells you about it once a year.

dossiers.de: Einundvierzig, Kanzleivorsteherin, seit 1953 im Haus: drei Minister, zwei Umzüge. Witwe seit 1957 — im Haus gilt das als lange her, ihr nicht. Den Ring trägt sie noch, rechts, was die Jüngeren für eine Marotte halten und die Älteren nicht. Sie ist die Einzige, die noch weiß, wie es vorher war, und sie sagt es bereitwillig, aber immer erst, wenn sie den Bogen zu Ende getippt hat. Bei ihr beschweren sich die anderen, weil sie zuhört, ohne etwas daraus zu machen. Ein Blatt, das noch zu retten ist, hat sie noch nie weggeworfen. Sie nennt das Sparsamkeit. Sie hat 1946 auch schon nichts weggeworfen.
dossiers.en: Forty-one, in the building since 1953: three ministers and two removals. Widowed since 1957 — the building considers that a long time ago; she does not. She still wears the ring, on the right hand, which the younger ones take for an eccentricity and the older ones do not. She is the only one who still knows how it used to be, and she will say so readily, but never before she has finished the sheet she is on. The others complain to her, because she listens without making anything of it. She has never thrown away a sheet that could still be saved. She calls it thrift. She didn't throw anything away in 1946 either.

dossiers.de: Verheiratet mit einem Mann bei der Bundesbahn, zwei Söhne: Der eine soll Ingenieur werden, der andere weiß schon, dass er keiner wird. Sie bringt Kuchen mit und behauptet jedes Mal, er sei diesmal nichts geworden. Sie weiß, wer ein Kind erwartet, wer umzieht und wer sich trennt, und sie erzählt es nur Leuten, die es ohnehin schon wissen. Das hält sie für Diskretion. Es ist auch welche, ungefähr.
dossiers.en: Married to a man on the railways, two sons: one is to become an engineer and the other already knows he won't. She brings cake and claims every time that it didn't turn out. She knows who is expecting, who is moving and who is separating, and she tells it only to people who know already. She considers this discretion. It more or less is.

dossiers.de: Achtundzwanzig, seit vier Jahren im Haus, verlobt seit Ostern. Geheiratet wird im Frühjahr, und was danach kommt, hat das Haus schon entschieden, ohne dass es jemand ausgesprochen hätte. Sie kleidet sich eine Gehaltsstufe über ihrer Gehaltsstufe und trägt dazu ein Gesicht, das zu einer Bemerkung einlädt. Gemacht hat sie noch niemand. Sie tippt gut und gern und redet dabei nicht, was sie für Höflichkeit hält und die anderen für Hochmut. Auf die Frage, ob sie danach bleibt, sagt sie „Mal sehen“, und zwar so, als hätte sie schon gesehen.
dossiers.en: Twenty-eight, four years in the building, engaged since Easter. The wedding is in the spring, and what happens after that the building has already decided without anyone saying it aloud. She dresses one salary grade above her salary grade and wears an expression that invites a remark. Nobody has made one yet. She types well and willingly and does not talk while she does it, which she considers courtesy and the others consider airs. Asked whether she will stay on afterwards she says we'll see, in the tone of somebody who has already seen.

dossiers.de: Putzfrau, Anfang fünfzig, seit Jahren im Haus und für die meisten hier ein Geräusch im Flur. Sie sieht mehr als alle anderen und macht sich nichts daraus, weil es sie nichts angeht und weil es, ehrlich gesagt, meistens nichts ist. Sie redet gern, wenn jemand stehen bleibt, und das tut fast nie jemand. Sie hat zwei erwachsene Kinder, von denen sie spricht wie von entfernten Bekannten, auf die sie stolz ist.
dossiers.en: The charwoman, in her early fifties, years in the building and to most of the people here a sound in the corridor. She sees more than anybody and makes nothing of it, because it is not her business and because, to be honest, it is usually nothing. She likes talking when somebody stops, and almost nobody stops. She has two grown children she speaks of the way you speak of distant acquaintances you are proud of.

dossiers.de: Sarah Wessen, Privatdetektivin in Bonn. An den meisten Tagen ein schlichter Wollmantel mit einem großen Knopf am Hals, die Sonnenbrille auch drinnen. Für das Ministerium zieht sie den roten Mantel mit dem Gürtel an und lässt die Sonnenbrille in der Tasche, denn ein Haus voller Beamter will einem in die Augen sehen. Im Laden an der Ecke ruft man ihr „die Detektivin mit dem Schnüffler“ hinterher. Sie lächelt charmant wie ein Fräulein vom Filmfunk, wenn es nützt, und sie hat ein zweites Lächeln, das heißt: Ich habe das schon zu Ende gedacht. Mit Leuten, die nicht reden wollen, geht sie um wie eine ältere Schwester, die den kleinen Bruder zum Reden bringen will. Ob jemand unschuldig ist, weiß sie nach ihrem eigenen untrüglichen Gefühl, lange bevor sie es belegen kann.
dossiers.en: Sarah Wessen, private detective in Bonn. Most days a plain wool coat with one big button at the throat, and the sunglasses stay on indoors. For the ministry she puts on the red coat with the belt and leaves the sunglasses in her bag, because a building full of officials wants to see a person's eyes. In the shop on the corner they call after her: the detective with the sniffer. She smiles charmingly, like a young lady off the film pages, when it is useful, and she has a second smile that means: I have already thought this through to the end. With people who would rather not talk she works the way an older sister works on a younger brother. Whether somebody is innocent she knows by her own unerring feeling, long before she can show it.

dossiers.de: Kommissar Friedrich Mauser von der Bonner Kriminalpolizei. Ein Mann, der seine Brille etwa siebzehnmal in der Stunde zurechtrückt und über den Rand hinwegsieht, wenn ihm etwas nicht passt. Das Hemd zerknittert, das Jackett rückt er sich zurecht, als säße eine Wespe darin. Hinter dem Schreibtisch sitzt er wie ein grummeliger Wachhund, und die Falten auf seiner Stirn werden tiefer, je länger man redet. Auf dem Tisch ein eingetrockneter Kaffeefleck, ein wachsender Papierstapel und ein Notizblock, der längst aussieht wie ein Kunstprojekt aus Tinte und Kaffeespuren. Wenn nichts anliegt, nimmt er sich alte ungelöste Akten noch einmal vor. Über gewisse Formulierungen sagt er, sie röchen noch deutlich nach der alten Zeit.
dossiers.en: Kommissar Friedrich Mauser of the Bonn criminal police. A man who straightens his glasses about seventeen times an hour and looks at you over the rim of them when something does not suit him. The shirt creased, the jacket tugged straight as though a wasp were sitting in it. Behind his desk he sits like a grumpy watchdog, and the furrows on his forehead deepen the longer you talk. On the desk a coffee stain two days dry, a growing pile of paper, and a notepad long since like an art project made of ink and coffee marks. When nothing is on, he goes back through the old unsolved files. Of certain turns of phrase he says you can still smell the old regime on them.

walk.cover: Sarah Wessen is a private detective (Privatdetektivin), and nobody in this building is to know it. Herr Grau of the Personalreferat asked Kommissar Mauser, off the record, for somebody quiet, and Mauser sent her. To everybody else she is looking at how paper moves through a ministry (wie das Papier durchs Haus läuft), so asking where a paper goes after somebody's desk is her job. Asking who knew what is not. People will give her a little of their time each day, and no more.

shrugs: "That," says Herr Simon, "is not a Registratur matter."
Herr Simon has nothing to add to that.
Herr Simon cannot help Sarah there.
people.looked: Herr Simon looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: Herr Simon has the afternoon's returns to put away (die Rückläufe).

hello.text: Files go out on the book and come back on the book, and roughly one a month does not, and each one of those he remembers.

lines.text: The return went across sealed and the seal was broken at the Finance Ministry. Herr Simon never had it open.

He has eaten in the canteen every working day for twenty years, and in all that time Frau Pohlmann has not once come down to it. The morning the return was first talked of at the pool's table, Frau Adam was the one asking everybody what it was.

When he takes files up to 407 the pool's girl is as often as not at the table on the landing for the post, and he has never seen her go in at Frau Pohlmann's door, or Frau Pohlmann come out to the table.
The stairs and the paternoster both pass the landing outside his counter. He sees the newest girl go up for the post most days, and he has not seen Frau Litt go up in years.

He locks the Registratur last thing. By then the pool is long gone, every one of them down the stairs past his counter, and the cleaners come up past it while he turns the key, the charwoman with them. In the morning he is at his counter before any of the pool comes in, and the cleaners have been and gone.
Asked what the enclosure column counts, he says whatever is in the envelope, and that it is there so a thing that goes out with three comes back with three, and that it has never meant anything else.

the pension file.talk: Herr Simon says he has given up putting it away: it would only be asked for again before he had sat down.

people.name: Frau Litt
shrugs: Frau Litt says that is not a question for the pool.
Frau Litt has nothing to add to that.
Frau Litt cannot help Sarah there.
people.looked: Frau Litt looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: Frau Litt says some of them have work to do.

hello.text: The new machines are lighter to strike and Frau Litt does not think that is an improvement, because a light touch lets you type faster than you can think. There are two of them so far, and they take the new ribbons that run through once; the rest of the pool is still on cloth.
The cloth ribbons went round and round and you used them until they were grey, and she can still tell you what a box of them cost in 1953, to the Pfennig, without being asked.

lines.text: She holds a spent ribbon up against the window for anybody in the pool who will stand still, and reads off it what was typed on it, and thinks it a scandalous waste to throw out a ribbon that has only been through the machine once.

She has not been up to the fourth floor in years and does not mean to start, so it is the newest girl in the pool who brings her down the spoiled sheets out of the fourth-floor sack, and only the sheets, because a sheet with a clean back is still half a sheet.
Frau Adam heard about the return the same morning as the rest of the pool, and was put out about it all week, which with Frau Adam you can see from across the room.
When it finally came out which three posts had gone, two of them belonged to women who were nowhere near the bottom of the list, and the room has not finished being astonished about it.
Herr Grau has never once sent down for a girl by name in all the years she has had this room. It is always a typist, and it is always through the outer office.

married.talk: Frau Litt says the girls always think it will be different for them.

people.name: Frau Adam
shrugs: Frau Adam has a great deal to say about it, none of it to the point.
Frau Adam has nothing to add to that.
Frau Adam cannot help Sarah there.
people.looked: Frau Adam looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: Frau Adam is wanted at her machine, and says so with regret.

hello.text: She heard about the return when everybody else did and was put out about it, and being put out about not knowing a thing first is the one thing she cannot act.
Her elder boy has finished and the younger one has not, and she tells you which of them she worries about and it is not the one you expect.
Coal has gone up again and she says the figure, and it is right.

Frau Litt had Fräulein Bühl up at that window with a spent ribbon inside a week of her starting, the same as she does with all of them, and Fräulein Bühl was politer about it than most of them are.

eats.talk: Frau Adam says she eats with everybody, and knows who does not.

grau.talk: Frau Adam says he is perfectly civil and she would not know him in the street.

stairs.talk: Frau Adam says she takes whatever is quickest, and it is never the stairs.

younger.evade: Frau Adam, for once, does not want to talk about it.

people.name: Fräulein Bühl
shrugs: Fräulein Bühl says she had not thought about it.
Fräulein Bühl has nothing to add to that.
Fräulein Bühl cannot help Sarah there.
people.looked: Fräulein Bühl looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: Fräulein Bühl has a letter to finish.

hello.text: Whoever is newest in the pool fetches the post from the fourth floor, and has done since before anybody can remember, and she is newest.
She is to be married next spring and means to go on working, which her mother thinks is a phase.
She will not use the paternoster and takes the stairs, and says so without being asked, the way people do about the things that frighten them.

post.talk: Fräulein Bühl says it is only the post, and somebody has to.

stairs.evade: Fräulein Bühl says she simply prefers them, and asks whether Sarah thinks it will rain.

return.evade: Fräulein Bühl says she only knows it is the week when nobody upstairs has time for anyone, and looks for her eraser.

married.evade: Fräulein Bühl goes pink, and says it is not settled, and then that it is.

the pension file.talk: Fräulein Bühl says she fetches what she is sent for, and has stopped asking what is in it.

people.name: the charwoman
shrugs: The charwoman says she only does the floors.
The charwoman has nothing to add to that.
The charwoman cannot help Sarah there.
people.looked: The charwoman looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: The charwoman has the whole floor still to do.

hello.text: She asked Herr Simon once, while he was locking up, why the thrown-out ribbons have the letters cut out of them in a row, and he showed her: the bar swings up, the ribbon is between it and the paper, and what the blow lifts off the ribbon is what comes out on the sheet.
She carries out what is in the baskets and does not read any of it, and would not have made much of it if she had, and says so without any embarrassment at all.
The trolley has a wheel that turns sideways and there is a form for it, and she has filled the form in twice.

lines.text: Frau Pohlmann tears her spoiled sheets up small before they go in the basket, every one of them, which nobody else in this building does, and it is the devil to get the pieces out of the corners.
Out of Frau Pohlmann's basket, every few weeks, the ribbon she has taken off her machine: the new shiny sort, not the cloth ones the pool throws out. It goes in the sack with the rest.

people.looked: The cook looks, and has nothing to say about it.
people.tired: The cook has the tickets to count.

hello.text: After five she counts the day's meal tickets into bundles of fifty, and one bundle is always one short, and she has stopped minding which.

people.tired: The porter has the door to see to.

He lets the cleaning women in at the side door himself, and not one of them has come in while anybody from the pool was still in the building: the pool goes out past his window first, and he sees to it. In the morning they are out again before the first of the pool is at the door.

topics.ask: Sarah asks what the first Referatsleiter in that office was like.
raised_by: Eleven years in that outer office and three Referatsleiter, and the first of them wrote everything in longhand and she typed from it, and she thought at the time that this was the last of something.

glossary.long: A list of everyone in a room in order of length of service, pinned up where they can all see it. It is not a list of who will be let go, and everybody reads it as one anyway.
A list of who is to be let go. The Dienstaltersliste is explicitly not one of these.
The Referat that deals with the staff themselves: appointments, transfers, leave, and who is let go.
A hundredth of a Mark. To know a price 'to the Pfennig' is to know it exactly, years later, without being asked.
The man in charge of a Referat, and of everything that comes into it.
The room that keeps the files, and books every one of them out and back in again. Nothing leaves it without a signature in the book.
The schedule of posts a ministry is allowed to have, settled once a year with the budget. A post struck off it is a job that stops existing.

The room in front of a senior man's own, where his secretary sits and through which everything reaching him passes. By the rules it begins with an Unterabteilungsleiter. The Personalreferat has, by exception, a typist of its own, and the house calls her room the outer office all the same.
A lift of open cars on a continuous loop that never stops. You step in as one passes and step out again at your floor. Plenty of people will not use one.
